newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Grain/Oilseeds - All quiet on the China front.
newsitem.headline: China Grain/Oilseeds - All quiet on the China front.

text.p: China's grain trading business has ground to a halt with little going in, nothing coming out and Chinese buyers waiting for prices to ease before placing orders for the remainder of the year, traders said on Thursday.
Canada seems to be the only recipient of Chinese grain business, having added 700,000 tonnes of wheat to confirmed sales of 800,000 tonnes, according to regional traders.
A People's Daily report that two million tonnes of corn was being shipped from Jilin province to relieve shortages in China's south failed to stir sceptical traders.
"There is plenty of corn around," a Hong Kong trader said.
"We talk to feed millers in the south and they have plenty of corn. If it was tight, you would have seen some movement in the (Dalian exchange) futures price," he said.
The November corn contract on the Dalian Commodity Exchange did not move from 1,410 yuan (US$170) a tonne on Wednesday, when the People's Daily report was published.
This price reflected a premium of 40 to 50 yuan ($4.80 to $6.0) a tonne over the cash price for poor quality corn in the northern Chinese port of Dalian, traders said.
By Thursday, the November contract price had fallen to 1,360 yuan ($163.80) a tonne.

Most corn in Dalian is said to be of deteriorating quality, as it has been sitting in warehouses since May awaiting an official go-ahead on corn exports. The light on exports, however, remains red and the opportunity for profit has passed.
"The government would only get involved if the situation is out of control and the state feed mills can't get enough corn for production," another trader said. "But this is not so."
Another source said some feed mills in the south not only had no trouble sourcing corn, an ingredient of animal feed, but looked hard for excuses to turn back contracts as they arrived.
Soybeans and soymeal were too expensive for Chinese buyers, traders said.
Chinese bean inquiries were hovering around $315-320 a tonne, well behind prevailing C&F prices from the United States to China of $335-340, traders said.
Interest in soymeal stopped at around $295 a tonne, traders said, still $10 short of the going market price.
Soybean oil is a different story, with Argentine traders reporting earlier this week that China was buying from Argentina and Brazil for nearby shipment.
"China has been buying. Every month they're buying a bit more, but it's not an explosion," one trader told Reuters in Buenos Aires.

China has been importing a minimium of 70,000 tonnes of South American soybean oil a month throughout 1996, for a total so far of about one million tonnes, a Hong Kong vegetable oil trader said. This was despite an apparent lack of official quotas, he said.
A rise in vegetable oil prices in China's interior reflected a gradual depletion in what had been high stocks, he and other trading sources said.
But figures released weekly by China's National Grains and Oils Information Centre show little recent price movement.

Reported soybean oil prices in Jilin were 7,000 yuan ($843) a tonne on Wednesday, compared with 7,400 yuan a week earlier. Vegetable oil in Hubei, central China, was reported by the centre on Wednesday at 6,870 yuan ($827) a tonne, compared to 7,100 yuan a week earlier.

Regional traders said, however, they expected China to return to the vegetable oil market within the next few months to ensure adequate stocks for the country's premier public holiday at Chinese New Year around February.
